I will now ask the usher to please escort you out of the courtroom and to bring the new witness in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, our next witness, could you tell us who our next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next witness is Lieutenant Colonel Hakan Birger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before this witness leaves, I think it eluded us all, the initialing of the map where there was a discussion about 2.000 metres. Maybe it would be good to have an IC number for it because there will be later references to whether it was 1 or 2 kilometres. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And what was on the ELMO for some reason was not entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The others are not a problem. The others are all in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar is telling me that the image must absolutely be marked. So, please, Witness, could you sit down. We will call up the photograph again on the screen. Thank you. Could you please mark on the screen today's date, March 26, 2007, and sign your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it be possible for me to zoom out on the map to look at the map data?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] We can show the witness the original so he can look at the distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will be given the original map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to correct myself. I said 2 centimetres is 1 kilometre. It is 4 centimetres is 2 kilometres, but it is still one square is 1 kilometre so it doesn't change the diameter. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] At the bottom of the map take a simple pencil and see, according to the scale, what the distance is from 0 to 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll give an IC number for the map on screen. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the map on the screen will become Exhibit IC --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute Just a minute, registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see my mistake. Sorry. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The witness did not mark the spot where the incident happened. I would like him to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks] THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could you please mark it with a number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Registrar, could you please give number for this map that we have now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will become IC 509.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: For the record it might be useful to state that in a map 1:50.000, which we have before us, 2 centimetres are equal to 1 kilometre in the terrain. In a map 1:100.000, it is 1 centimetre which corresponds to 1 kilometre. I do not think that this is something which is not really a matter of common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please. The date is May 25 or May 26? I think the date is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this were May 26th today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or March 26th today, says the interpreter. March 26th, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, you put March 25, and we're at March 26th today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm also very sorry I have to correct myself again on the distance on the map because I was too quick with my conclusion. The reason for it is I usually work with military maps that have 1-kilometre squares, but these have indeed 2-kilometre squares, because it's usually with 88, 89, 90, and here it's only the even numbers that are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The map on the screen now dated March 26th, 2007, is number IC 509. Mr. Kovacic, do you want an IC number also for the map itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be a good idea for technical reasons. This is good enough for us, especially after the witness has made the correction in his statement about the distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... necessary. Witness, now, after this correction, thank you. And could the usher please escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you now have the floor for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next witness is lieutenant colonel Hakan Birger. And perhaps if I could suggest that once he's brought in and placed under oath perhaps if we could then take the break before I begin the direct examination I believe I could then structure it in such a way that I could finish the direct examination before we finish for the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Time, regarding time, the Prosecution had planned on an hour and 30 minutes. We decided that the Defence would be allocated two hours, and it's up to the accused to split the time among themselves. Maybe to prevent any problem we could have the break right now? We'll have a 20-minute break right now and then we will resume after the break. I think this is a batter way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I can see that the witness is in the courtroom. Please, Mr. Registrar, have the witness be taken out of the room, just for a matter of seconds. Please leave the room, sir. Sir, you're going to leave the courtroom just for a few seconds. I have to make an announcement without you being in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. With regard to the length, we decided that the Defence would have two hours. I said that you had to agree among yourselves. If there's no agreement, we will think that General Petkovic should have 30 minutes, General Praljak 30 minutes, and as to the other counsel, they will each have 15 minutes. This is how we're going to spread the time. Secondly, I'm saying this to you without the witness being in the courtroom because last time Mr. Karnavas, who is not with us today, said that when the witness knew in advance how much time he had to answer questions this could have an impact on his testimony. So from now on we shall no longer say how long the time will be when the witness is in the courtroom, because we don't want him or her to how much time is left for questions and to answer them. So this is what I wanted to say. This is the reason why I asked the witness to go out the courtroom. Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for giving me this opportunity. I would like to make a verbal request to enable the Defence to have a longer time for examining this witness for the same reason. The Prosecution intends to spend 90 minutes on direct examination exclusively on evidence that they intend to introduce through this witness. Apart from that, there will be statements introduced totaling 30 pages of text. Mere reading of these statements would require around 90 minutes without interpretation, and for answers to be elicited in direct examination, the Prosecution would need approximately four to five hours for the same content and testimony, so that in viva voce, the Prosecution would need five to six hours for this evidence. I would therefore kindly ask for the Defence to have the whole day tomorrow for cross-examination, which is around four and a half hours, and we will distribute this time between us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have the 65 ter list in front of me, but I was under the impression that initially there was one hour and a half for the Prosecution on that list. So the Defence was aware of the time allotted. I know that the Prosecutor intended to have a 65 ter -- or, rather, to have a 92 ter witness, but then you decided to remain viva voce. So this is what is happening. I'm just leafing through the documents as you were speaking, and their a number of documents we have already seen and that we're bound to see again. However, there is the 2980 document, which is of several pages, but as a matter of fact, we are interested in the 23rd of October, and that's not 30 pages long. So personally, this is what I wanted to convey to you. But, Mr. Mundis, you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Let me -- I'll accept full responsibility for perhaps what has resulted in some confusion. As I indicated in a letter that was submitted to the Defence and a copy of which was provided to the Trial Chamber's legal officers this morning, we indicated that due to time pressure and concerns about completing the schedule for this week that we were considering or were likely to employ the 92 ter procedure with respect to the next witness. Given the fact that we seem to have now completed the first witness and there are no longer those time pressures - I did indicate this to at least one of the Defence teams earlier - we are prepared to go ahead with a viva voce examination of this witness. I will also state that although a number of documents were initially listed as against this witness and are in the bundles that have been provided at least to the Trial Chamber, I expect to only be using approximately 10 of those documents with this witness because the remaining documents have either been already covered or the witness didn't have sufficient knowledge or information concerning those documents. So I am at this point prepared to go forward taking this witness as a viva voce witness and showing him approximately 10 documents. And as I indicated prior to the break, I do believe that we will complete the direct examination by close of business today or perhaps have a little bit of time remaining for tomorrow but not any significant amounts of time remaining for tomorrow. So I would propose going forward as a viva voce witness and using approximately 10 documents with the witness, and I certainly believe I can do that within approximately 90 minutes, barring any unforeseen circumstances. I believe that the witness's two prior statements could be among the bundle that was provided to the Trial Chamber, but again I will take him as a viva voce witness under the current plan because of the fact that we completed Lieutenant van der Weijden testimony in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can only express my satisfaction at having this witness heard viva voce. That will reduce our needs for time, but not much, for the very simple reason that this witness will utter a sentence and a document will be shown to him for which I will need at least one hour to show the real state of affairs. So that if my estimate was four hours for cross-examination, that can now be reduced to three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may point out one matter that is perhaps technical in one aspect. Regardless of whether there was a 92 witness or viva voce witness, if the Prosecution succeeds in finishing with the witness in 90 minutes or so, then the Defence would have all day tomorrow, approximately, because the witness after is not scheduled until the day after tomorrow. We are at risk of facing an absurd situation where we would leave tomorrow two -- or two and a half hours earlier, before the end of the day, without having examined the witness properly. At this stage of the Prosecution case, I may say that the Prosecution's planning is almost perfect. We had no idle time almost. But there were some witnesses who were introduced at a late stage, like Mr. van der Weijden, and the time was too short for us to properly prepare for cross-examination. This witness comes with two statements, as my colleague said, the statements having been taken at different times and for purposes of different cases as is the custom of the Prosecution. There are statements from 1995, which in terms of content and lines of questioning was destined to serve the indictment concerning a conflict between Croats and Muslims, and another statement from 2000, or maybe 2001, that was designed to support another case. I believe it was Hadzihasanovic. So now, if we are going forward with 92 ter, then both statements should be taken into account. If it's a viva voce witness, then we will have to cross-examine on the second statement let alone the other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis said that it will be a viva voce witness. Is that so, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, unless we spend considerably more time arguing about how little time there is available, I am prepared to go forward on a viva voce basis and show this witness 10 documents. I expect that it will take no more than 90 minutes to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're going to start, as we indicated. Tomorrow we'll have four hours. If indeed you need extra time, speaking about General Petkovic, he will have the extra time. Let us bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps while the usher is doing that, Mr. President, there were a number of issues, or at least one issue in particular that was remaining from our hearing late last week that the Defence teams wanted the accused present for in order to discuss that issue. I might suggest that if there were some time towards the end of this week that might be an appropriate time to discuss that, because the next three weeks or the entire calendar in April appears to be relatively tight, and if the Chamber wants to come back to that issue and if there is some time towards the end of this week, that might be the best time to deal with that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Could you please state your surname, first name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Hakan Birger, and I'm born in 1955, 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm an officer in the Swedish army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, have you had an opportunity to testify in this Tribunal and, if so, in which case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you had -- I shall repeat. Have you had an opportunity to testify in this Tribunal and, if so, could you tell us in which case you testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's no problem for me. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a rather simple question. I asked you whether you have been a witness in this Tribunal. So say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I've been here before, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since you said yes, maybe you could tell me in which case you were a witness, in case you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I witness here in case about -- it was officers and generals from the 3rd Corps and the, say, the Muslims' brigade from the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have testified once before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You testified in the Hadzihasanovic, Kubura case. I shall ask you to read out now the solemn declaration you have in your hands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please sit down. Since you've been a witness before, you know the proceedings before this Tribunal. First questions will be put to you by the Prosecution. They believe they should complete their examination-in-chief today, and tomorrow you will have to answer questions put to you by the Defence counsel representing the accused or by the accused themselves. You have four Judges in fronts of you. They, too, can ask questions of you. We can ask questions at any time, but we have now decided to wait until questions have been put by both parties to ask questions ourselves, unless it is absolutely necessary, in which case we will put questions to you because we should not necessarily wait until all parties have put their questions. Please try to respond very clearly. You are a military man. I'm sure you'll do that. And if you do not understand a question asked of you, do not hesitate to say so and ask the person putting the question to reformulate it, as you have just done with me. So this is generally speaking how the proceedings will unfold. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Lieutenant-Colonel Birger. Could you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry. Let's start, sir, if you will, telling the Trial Chamber a little bit about what you were doing in terms of your military career in early 1993. What post were you serving in, in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: In early 1993, I was a battalion commander in the Swedish army, and I was also working as a teacher in academy for officers' training and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, sir, when you received orders to report to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I was there voluntary and all officers and soldiers were there voluntary, so it -- it was what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when did you volunteer to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I think it was in the beginning of May 1993, and we start training and we recruit the soldiers in June, and we start training in the beginning -- first three weeks in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was the position that you held during this deployment to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I was company commander for one of the mechanised company, 8 mechanised company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And within what military organisation were you deployed to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was a mechanised battalion, and we have three mechanised companies in this battalion, and also one supply and staff company, and it was also a Danish tank company in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what was the name of this battalion that you were serving in as a company commander?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. We had one battalion in Macedonia before, so it was NordBat 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant Colonel Birger, can you tell the Trial Chamber when you first entered Bosnia and Herzegovina and for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I think it was the 13 of May -- middle of September. It was down where we were recognised with the battalion commander, the company commander and some staff members. We were -- used the Swedish air force to Italy and next day we was flying to Sarajevo and was down there a week, and after that we were flying back to Denmark. In Denmark our unit was for training, the last training before going to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Lieutenant Colonel Birger, when did your company deploy to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was me and my platoon leader. We was totally 10 in my company. We came down into Bosnia the last day in September 1993 to Tuzla, and the next day, the 1st of October, we used our cars and get down to Vares [Realtime transcript read in error "various"] area and there we was living together with engineering company from the Canadian Battalion. And the 1st Platoon of my alpha platoon arrived to Bosnia down to this area the 20 of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when did the other platoons --

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I think it was the 22nd or something like this, the -- they arrived -- I don't remember exactly but they arrived -- I have the three mechanised platoons in October, 1 and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I just wanted to point out a mistake in the transcript, page 57, line 25. It says "various area." I think the witness actually said Vares area, which seems important to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To the Vares area?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us again, sir, when the remaining platoons of the 8th company or 8th Mechanised Company of NordBat arrived?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: We arrived as they starting in the 20 -- 20 of October the first platoon arrived and when they arrived some days later, and I think in this time, I mean in the last day of October, have Alpha, Bravo, and Charlie platoon in my area. That's 3 mechanised infantry platoons. And later we also have my anti-tank missile platoon, but they arrived in November some days without vehicles, and they came in -- in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell the Trial Chamber please a little bit about the composition of each of your platoons to include the type of vehicles and equipment that they had during this deployment?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was Swedish -- Swedish old APCs. It was from 60s, beginning of 60s, and it was tracked APCs with 20 millimetres automatic cannon. We have Carl Gustaf anti-tank weapon. We have machine guns, and we have carbines, so to say, yeah, weapon, hand weapon hand. We also have -- we was equipped for war, so to say, in Swedish organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately how many men were in each of the platoons?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: A little bit more than 30 and totally in the company we was 150, and I have also directly in October one so to say unit from a medical platoon. So I have also nurse and doctors in my company the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And before I forget to ask you this, sir, how long was the 8th mechanised company deployed with NordBat in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was long time. They change person in -- we changed. We had the same name, same name of battalion, the same name of company, so we start rotate -- we rotated personnel in last March and beginning of April 1994. So more or less six months.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We've been asked by the interpreters to slow down. Can you please tell us Lieutenant Colonel Birger about your reporting chain of command going upwards?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Our battalion staff was in factory just outside Tuzla and where we have a battalion staff and the staff and supply company and the battalion commander. So I reporting to this place and the battalion reporting to the BH command in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, what was the name of the NordBat commander, the battalion commander, in Tuzla during your deployment?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was Colonel Ulf Henricsson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you explain, sir, to avoid any confusion, what was BH command in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: BH command what -- when we arrived it was UN command for the UN commands in Bosnia, and when it was also in Zagreb it was headquarter for UNPROFOR in whole Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So BH command was part of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. It was a part and they command the UN battalions in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Birger, during the time your company was deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who was the BH commander, the commander of BH command?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: When I arrive it was General Briquemont from Belgium, and after some months, I don't really exactly know, we changed commander to Sir Michael Rose from United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, sir, where you located your headquarters upon arriving in Vares?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: We look for place so we could -- we know the winter could be very hard in this area so we look for place where we could raise tent inside buildings, and we find that place outside Vares more or less north of Vares in -- in a factory. And this factory, it was also sawmill, and it was also factory for furnitures. And the last place, the place for furnitures factory, so it was good for us so we have agreement with the -- they were, what you can say, local government in Vares how we should pay and so on. So we rent this place for the Vares company -- Vares government, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was your location known to the local people as the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes, it was close to the sawmill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about any buildings that were adjacent to the sawmill or outside the sawmill at this location?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the commander for the forces in this area what they call Bobovac Brigade, this headquarter was very close. I think it's also only 200 metres from the gate to the sawmill, and it was, what I could understand, a hotel, maybe a sports hotel or something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the Bobovac Brigade. Can you tell us which military force the Bobovac Brigade belonged to?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It's belonged to who you ask. If we ask the commander of the 2nd Corps up in Tuzla they said it was a part of a 2nd Corps. But if I asked the commander of the Bobovac Brigade, he said it was more or less an independent unit in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say the 2nd Corps, which army or armed force are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you familiar with a military force known as the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Familiar -- I don't understand exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you know about an armed force known as the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, about the situation from a military point of view at the time of your arrival in Bosnia-Herzegovina in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. What I could understand, the Swedish government was want to have a more or less battalion up in Tuzla area, so to -- to have the company down in Vares area, it was more or less something down to Swedish government want, but when we came down where we were under command of UN command, so they want to have one company in Vares area, and what we understand it was, it could be war or fighting in this area and it was a problem. There was also a lot of refugees. When I came there first day I arrived to Vares when we was down in September, first I observed there was a lot of refugees inside the town, thousands of them, and I understand that most of them came from Kakanj area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what about the actual situation from a military point of view? Was there active combat in your area?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: We find out in October that it was no problem in north and east. What's mean, it was a brigade in Olovo was a part of 2nd Corps. When we talked to this brigade commander and ask him about Bobovac Brigade, they said it's no -- they was more or less friends. We will have a meeting to solve small problem every week, and I have observed and we understand that in west it was fighting, more or less small fighting against 3rd Corps, the Bosnian 3rd Corps, Bosnian army 3rd Corps. And when I ask him he said yes he understand it was fighting. And we went because I think he also said, they really crazy, the 3rd Corps. So I understand they were fighting. It was also fighting a little south-west of Vares, and some day we have arrived it was some policemen and some policemen who are be -- some policemen was killed and some was wounded, and my medical look -- the day after we visit the -- this policemen, and they was in what you can call a field hospital, and it was in the 2nd Corps area west of -- north-west of Olovo. So I think it was more friendly with the 2nd Corps because the 2nd Corps said it was a part of 2nd Corps, but not on the 3rd Corps. That was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so that the record is clear, sir, who was fighting against the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Bobovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what was the geographic extent of your company's AOR or area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- it was very big. We -- we -- from the south we have to the confrontation line or to the border to the BH army and up to Kladanj. It's a place north of Olovo. And up in the area of Ribnica and down to Kopjari and down to south of -- south-west of Vares. So it was very big area for one company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than the Bobovac Brigade and the 2nd and 3rd Corps of the army of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what other military forces, if any, were in or near your AOR?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Sometimes I don't really not understand what the type of unit was from the south. They tell us it was the 6th Corps and it was the 1st Corps, but in November and the rest of my time there it was the 1st Corps in south, and it was more or less they call it Sarajevo corps, they call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, which army was that?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: BH army. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, were there any Bosnian Serb army or VRS forces in or around your AOR?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes, in Olovo there was more or less heavy fighting, and some days in the winter we could -- some were about 2.000 impacts in Olovo and it was fighting with the BSA army and the BH army. So it was also Serbs just east of Dastansko. Dastansko is a village east of Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Birger, during your first, say, month of being deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you have any interaction with the leadership of the Bobovac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: In the first weeks we have a good cooperation with the Bobovac Brigade. We was interest to know where -- the first thing for us, the important thing for us was to have freedom of movement, because if we don't have freedom of movement, we couldn't do anything. So that was very important for us. And that was no problem with the Bobovac Brigade. We have freedom of movement, and we was the first two weeks, maybe three, we was out more or less every day to -- to recognise in the different roads and different areas for observe -- where we could have observation posts, where are we could check points later, where we could even recognise positions for the Danish tank, because one of my missions was also to protect this area. I mean, the Tuzla finger up. So if not, the Serbs were cutting this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With whom did you have discussions in the Bobovac Brigade concerning freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: We had a meeting with -- with commander, and -- but the officers who was more or less showing us the maps who some days also following us out in the terrain what we call the operational officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall the names of the commanding officer and the operations officer?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I think it was Emil Harah, or something like this, was the commander, and Kresimir Bosic, something like this, was the operational officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the names of any other Bobovac Brigade officers that you had regular contact with?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: No. I remember they call one was security officer, and he could speak a little bit English, but I'm not really exactly remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you similarly have any contacts or discussions with anyone from the BH army 2nd or 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We have the same discussion with the brigade commander in Olovo, and also want to have freedom of movement, and we was there and more or less every time when we was there was impact close to our vehicles from the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Birger, did there come a time in October 1993 when the situation in your AOR became much more hostile or intense, in terms of the parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. I -- it was very important for me to -- soon I have my first soldiers down there to take them up in Kopjari area, and I had two reasons for that. First was to observe what's going on in the area, and the second was to observe down into village, Mijakovic and Dragovic, because it was more clear Muslims village inside this area, and I -- I want to observe so nothing happening with these people, and they have no food where it was -- they have a little bit bad situation in these two village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the approximate date that you went to this area, Kopjari?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes, I was there one of these first weeks in -- when I arrived we was up, and recognised also visit these two village, and immediately when I have down my Alpha platoon in this 20 of October, I at the afternoon take them up to this area, and -- and they have a position just south of Kopjari up on the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this position just south of Kopjari up on the hill?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: They was there to observe and report what was going on in the area and also to observe the -- down in the two village so nothing should happening with Muslims inhabitants in these two village. And I remember it was dark when I leave this place this evening, the 20 of October, and I talk to one might have officers when we walk to the car, and I said I think it's going on very quickly, because we also have observed the same day. It was a lot of BH soldiers down in Dragovic and Mijakovic and there were no soldiers there some weeks before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I believe, sir, just for the record you mentioned Dragovici and Mijakovici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the situation in the area around Kopjari and Dragovici, Mijakovici change in the next day or two?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yeah. The next day think it was early in the morning before I wake up I had waked up my staff soldiers and they was under fire, my soldier were was under fire in Kopjari, and the BH army had start an attack and they attacked at first from west a little bit north of Kopjari but the main, the big attack, so to say, came from this two village. And it was also fog in this morning, so -- they use this, so they came very close to the Kopjari and after some hours the village was taken by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did your Alpha platoon maintain an observation post on the hill near Kopjari?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: They was there until about -- until I send -- I don't know how long time they been in there, but in November sometimes we take them away, but these belong to the -- all the lines have changed in this moment one month later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But in the October November period you still maintained an observation post?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn now, sir, to the morning of 23 October 1993. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you remember happening on the morning of 23 October 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: This morning I was up in the meeting or I went -- I get up to -- to the Bobovac Brigade because we also have a meeting one day before about the situation in Kopjari area and so on, so we have a new meeting this morning, and when I came up there, there was no commanders. So nobody want to talk to me, and -- sorry, I -- sorry. It was later. I meet the commanders and they say it was in fight and they was in the war and been attacked from the south and that was correct because we have observed detonations and so on from the south. And the village of Mir, I think it was a village inside the Bobovac Brigade area, was attacked by the BH army. And they also informed me that therefore they have attacked a village with name Stupni Do, and they do that because there was shooting against the supply lines. The supply line was through this village down to Mir. I don't know before what this should be some Muslim village or something like this, so I don't really this moment understand. I think it was solely from BH army who had taken this village. So in the fighting was not -- nothing for us. We was not there to stop the war. We was there to protect the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say it was a soldier from the BH army who had taken this village, which village are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: My mean, BH army was attacking Mir and what I understand was also some soldiers inside Stupni Do shooting to the Bobovac Brigade supply lines. That was what they tell me in this morning. So therefore the Bobovac Brigade has start attack the Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say, sir, that was what they tell me in the morning, who was the "they"?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was the leader of the operational officer of the Bobovac Brigade. Brigade commander wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again the name of the operation officer?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I think it was Kresimir Bozic or something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, approximately what time on the 23rd of October, 1993, Kresimir Bozic told you this?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I don't really negotiation but I think it was maybe 8.00 or something like this. We have a normal routines in the camp, so maybe I -- or maybe between 7.30, 8.00, leave my camp and get up. It take only minutes. It was very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, approximately how long you remained at the Bobovac Brigade headquarters on the morning of the 23rd of October --

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I was maybe there only 20, 30 minutes because the commander wasn't there and they said they was in fighting in this area, and they have a lot to do and so on. So I leaved, and when I came back to my camp I have a reporting about some minutes after I have arrived that my soldiers who was going up to Kopjari was stopped by a check-point inside Vares, and this check-points have been opened before because we have agreement with Bobovac Brigade for freedom of movement. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately what time was this?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was maybe 9.00. It was just -- it was before lunchtime, I remember. And I get down there and talk to this -- you can call them policemen or what they was, and ask them why we don't -- was allowed to pass the check-point and they said it was for our safety, UNPROFOR safety because there was attack in Vares. I said that is my problem. That is not your problem. But they have order to stop UN units. So I ordered my soldiers to stay there and you are here until they let you go up to Kopjari or I give you another order. And that immediately I went back to Bobovac Brigade and talk to why we don't have freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you returned to the Bobovac Brigade, Lieutenant Colonel Birger, who did you speak with?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I speak to what we call the security officer or they called him -- we call him like this. Not the operation officer. And he could little English and we was not in the normal room, so to say. Normally we have meetings in -- you can call it an operational room with maps and so on. Now it was -- it was inside, the right side of the building. Now we were putting into the left, into a restaurant. And where we were sitting, and I want to talk to the commanders, but they said -- he only said, "No, no. We have no commanders. It's bad day for us today," and so on. And after some -- between coffee we have lunch there, and one hour get, two hours, and after some hours he said, "Maybe now we have people here from Kiseljak." And I asked what it was, two people, but I don't really understand what he mean about people from Kiseljak, but in afternoon I could observe it, arrive people. I don't know how many, but they arrived directly from a door past the restaurant and get inside to operational room, and it was people I never seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time on that morning speak to the people who came, who passed by this door?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time on that day speak to any of the people who passed by that door?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Not -- not this morning. Not on the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain at the Bobovac Brigade at this point in time on 23 October 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I was there just -- I think it was going to the end of afternoon, it's going to be dark, so I understand that nobody want to talk to me. No commanders was there, they said, so -- but I understand some commanders were coming from Kiseljak area but nobody want to talk to me. So I couldn't be there. So I leaved and get back to my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately how long were you there on that day, the 23rd of October?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I think it was about totally five to six hours. I don't really remember, but I was there just before lunch, or lunchtime, and get back just before it was starting to be dark outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And before I neglect to ask you this, sir, you mentioned that -- that the security officer spoke a little bit of English.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how you generally communicated with the leadership of the Bobovac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Normally we have interpreters. We have interpreters in our unit, and then later we also have a so-called local interpreters from Tuzla area and other areas. But in this moment we just have arrived to Bosnia, so we only have interpreters from Sweden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the situation was like when you returned to your headquarters at the sawmill on the 23rd of October in the late afternoon, early evening?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes, I can, but I have to add one more. When I remember when I was sitting in this restaurant I also could see they came with wounded soldiers, and what he informed me, this security officer, he came from fighting area just around Stupni Do. He was black dress, black in the face. When I arrived to my company, I -- I haven't been there so long time because I have my equipment off my body because I -- we have a movie of this -- from a video movie, because just after I arrived my battalion commander arrived from south. So he informed me about the situation he had observed from south, and the Bosnian army check-point in the south had been -- there have within some impact with mortar, and he -- when he passed by there was a die cow and a die old man lying beside the road. And he also observed up in the mountain, so to say, he came from south up to Vares. On the right side he could observe up in mountain it was red and smoke. So he could -- he understand that something was burning, very big area was burning. So when he came to my camp he said to me, "Do you know you have a village probably in your area who is burning?" "Yes, I know, and I think the name of this is Stupni Do."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall lieutenant Colonel Birger approximately what time Colonel Henricsson arrived at the sawmill headquarters?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: No, I don't know which time it was. It was dark outside. It was raining and I don't know. And -- but we start talking. We have to do something. And he have already talk -- if I remember right, talked to the BH army in south, and now he want to -- to inform me what -- we must do something. And we discuss that very much, look at the map, and we have a long discussion in mandatory terms what we have to do. And we decided to -- to try to stop fighting from the both side, and after that get into Stupni Do for look what's happening, especially with the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Having had this discussion with the NordBat commander, sir, what steps did you take?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we understand that we have to do something to get inside, so before that we also have to -- to have stop fighting. So we went down to the BH army, small headquarters or something. I think it was in Pajtov Han or something like this, south of Vares, and my commander was talking to these others, I don't talk to them. But he have some type of agreement that if we could get inside Stupni Do they should stop fighting for hours or something like this. So it was no problem. After that we went north, passed into the Bobovac Brigade area up to the Bobovac Brigade and have a meeting there with the leadership but it was little bit strange. It was not -- we don't meet normally brigade commander. It was new man from Kiseljak, and -- and he had a moustache, and he said his name was Ivica Rajic. And the operational officer we have meet before was also there, and we start negotiations with him but it was not so easy, because -- in the beginning it was no problem. We could get out to Stupni Do. We could do everything. And when he understand we have to do it this night, he said no. So we was discussing and the whole time he build up his steps, instead to find a solution little bit down. So it was impossibility to have agreement with him. So we leaved. And I remember he was walking out and he said, "If you get out Stupni Do tonight I'm going to stop you. I'm going to fight." And we said, "Okay, we understand what you are saying but we are going to get into Stupni Do."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately what time was this discussion or what time did you leave on the 23rd of October 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It's been very late. I think it was just before midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where did you and Colonel Henricsson go at that time.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: We went back to my camp and we discuss again, and immediately when we leave Bobovac Brigade, I give order with radio to my soldiers to be ready to -- with trucks and vehicles, armed vehicles to go out to Stupni Do. So when we come back they were more or less ready to go, but we discussed in the car and we discuss about risks for us. We have never been in this area. It was dark. It was fog outside. It was -- so to say it was not good weather for us. It was not good situation where we could use our weapons. It was more good weather for, say, light armed soldiers. So later we decided to wait until it was darkness the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, approximately how many men from your company were available on that evening of the 23rd of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I don't remember. It was more or less maximum one platoon or when we have also some truck, and -- but it was not so much. Maybe five, six vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where were the rest of the members of your company at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: We have -- I have soldiers out in -- in -- in Kopjari. I think it was one -- one part of one platoon. I have a lot of soldiers still in the Pancevo base in Belgrade. So it was more or less three platoons, mechanised platoons, inside. Maybe it was only two. I don't really remember. Maybe the second one have arrived the 22nd. So it could be three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, just to avoid confusion later, when you made reference to a lot of soldiers still in the Pancevo base in Belgrade, what were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: They was preparing a way to get inside Bosnia, and it was again the whole time with the Bosnian Serbs. We have -- it was not so easy to take inside these soldiers. They stop us the whole time. It was in November, I think, they stop all APCs. So the rest came from Croatia in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. I take it, sir, your vehicles were shipped by rail to Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, from Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Lieutenant Colonel Birger, what steps you took beginning the next morning --

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: The 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- to try to get to Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: We used the road down in Vares and in the south part of -- little bit south of the centre where is the bridge over the road and -- and when you take the road up to -- to Stupni Do, and you also have to pass under the railway. And this tunnel was closed so to say. There were anti-tank mines and it was soldier there with anti-tank weapons. So when we came there they stop us and said we was not allowed to pass. And we -- I remember I talked to them and tried to find a negotiation, because it was more or less no problem for us to use violence and go up, because I immediately could see we could passed over the railway, so to say, left of this tunnel, but we don't do that because we don't want to stop fighting. It was not Bafobe [phoen] was there. So I tried to negotiate and it was impossibility. They said, "No, you are not allowed to pass." I tried to talk to their commander, Bobovac Brigade. Nobody was there to talk to me. I send a part of my 2nd platoon up in another way. I know it was one road I think more or less from north down to Stupni Do to find this road, and he -- he reported later -- a bit later in the day he was stopped also in the check-point. And after I understand they was very, very close to Stupni Do. We have -- leave the vehicles. Get out. Some -- maybe they could observe down in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain down with your platoon that was by the -- the railroad tunnel?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: They was there the whole day. We tried to get out and there was also some young -- we could call them -- they was equipped like soldiers, but they was young and they was more or less -- I don't understand what it was for type of soldiers, but they belong -- there was Croats, and they came down there just after we have arrived and said, "This is not your country. Leave here," and they unload the workmen and so on. And my military police protect me and also been ready to open fire, and after some minutes we leaved and I talked to the policemen there and they said you must be careful about this soldier, because they are dangerous, and he also think -- he explained they came from Kakanj area and their family members have been killed and so on. And he also said, "I'm sorry to say, but I think you also have some type of these people in your country, but you have them in prison," or -- and I remember I tell him that, "You are a policeman. Take them. Arrest them and take them to prison." But he sard, "No, that's impossible, they kill me."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, there might be an error in the transcript on line 11 of this page. It indicates they unload the workmen and so on and my military police protected me. What did these -- this soldier or soldiers do when they approached you?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: They have Kalashnikov in their hands and they do something like this to -- ready to shoot and walking to -- forward me. And therefore my policemen get in front of me to protect me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how was this situation diffused?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. They -- after some minutes they leaved, and -- and I also leaved, get up back to the Bobovac Brigade headquarter, try to -- to find the commanders, to talk to them, to find a solution, but nobody commander was there. I don't remember how long time, how many times I was there, but I -- I remember I also have sent a patrol with a corps, only one officer and a driver with a car up at the road to Kopjari because over this road when you came, as I said, you could look down in Vares. You also could look over Vares. So we maybe could observe what's going on in Stupni Do. So I travel up to this officer to talk to him about the situation, and when I was there, there came a lady, maybe was 40, 45 years old, and she could speak a little bit German. So she inform us about the situation down in Vares, and she said it was more than 200 Muslims, young boys and men, inside the school just beside the mayor house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Had you heard of this before?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: No. It was new information for me, so I went back to Vares and get into the police station and I was very tough when I come inside there. I said, "I know and you know what's going on in this school. I want to have a list of all the prisoners and I want to have it now." And they immediately gave me a list and I could see that the left of every name it was a number, and I follow quickly down, and I have only a chance to look some seconds because they understand, I think, it was not so good for them to let me look at that. So just before they take it away from me again I have summarying down and could see it was about 233 numbers of prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time on the 24th of October, 1993, you were at the police station?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was at the afternoon, but not exactly the time, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in the police station on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I -- I know what I -- they give me coffee and so, and I said to them, "But now I want to have --" I would get inside this it and they said, "No, you are not allowed." I said if I'm not allowed I want to talk to one commander who can give me the -- he say that I'm allowed to get inside. But he said, "No, no, no, you couldn't talk to a commander." So I been angry and take my helmet and smash it in the table, and said, "No, I want to talk to your commander." And he immediately take the telephone and talk to somebody, but he's outside here and I could hear he was very, very angry, and he said, "You couldn't talk to him. He don't want to talk to you, and you're not allowed to get inside this school." So when I came out one of my soldiers informed me what it was, somebody who want to talk to you. So I went back. It was dark now outside and I went back my -- one of my APCs on the square and talk to -- and just to -- I think it was two members of the Bobovac Brigade. It was two HVO soldiers. And they -- they asked me, "Do you know what's going on in this school?" And I said, "Yes, I think so. I know that there are Muslim men and boy inside there." And he said, "If you are the UN commander here in Vares, you have to do something, because I am from this town and I don't want going bad for them," and then he walked away in the darkness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know who this person was?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: No, I have never meet him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, Lieutenant Colonel Birger, approximately how far this school was from the police station?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Oh, it's a small square, and you have the mayor house and -- in the square, and you have the school and if you look here you have the mayor house and back in you have the small police station. It was also a very little police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did you go after having this encounter with this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At your APC?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I don't really remember. Maybe I also once more tried to talk to the Bobovac Brigade, but I have no meeting just then, but I ordered in this minute that if we're not allowed won't get inside, we want to have APC outside. So I ordered that one APC from the 1st Platoon to stay down in the tunnel just close to the HVO check-point to try to get through up to Stupni Do. I had a Red Cross APC outside the school because I don't want to provocate. So therefore I had a Red Cross APC out there, and they have only -- mission for one was only observe, do nothing, only observe. I also have -- have some information earlier this day that it was Muslim people down in the village of Dastansko and there was also one musky [phoen]. So earlier this day have ordered had platoon who have been tried to find a way north of Stupni Do. It was the 2nd Bravo platoon. So two of these vehicles was down in Dastanko, and they stay there this evening to protect civilians, protect musky and so on, and observe, of course, what's going on in Dastansko. I also have one APC outside Dastansko up on the hill but I don't remember the name or the place but it was good place to observe the area. And of course I have one -- I have soldiers still up in Kopjari. So when I have all of that and give all of that and everybody was out, I have a new meeting this time at the evening. I don't really know the -- exactly time but it was at the evening. We were in Bobovac Brigade. It was not -- Ivica Rajic was not there. It was -- the battalion commander was not there, but I talk to the operational officer, and I understand more or less maybe he now was the, to say, the new brigade -- the new commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again for the record, sir, can you giver us the name?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: The operational officer Kresimir Bozic, something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And it's your understanding that he became the brigade commander at -- at about this time?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander that I understand. And we -- I have -- I tried to get into the school. I wanted to visit this prison. He said no. And the message to me from him was that you have to take all your soldiers inside the camp, and if you don't do that we're going to destroy them. And we are also going to -- shooting at your camp. The camp was not already a camp. It was still a factory. We have moved one day before, all of us in the 34 -- 33 [sic] of October. We do nothing to protect ourself. So it was still a factory with my units inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Lieutenant Colonel Birger, when you mentioned that you moved, and I think that was the -- can you give us the date that you moved?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I think we move the 23rd of -- of -- of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell it the Trial Chamber where you moved from --

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: From the sawmill --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- or to?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was the same factory area but I moved 100, 200 metres from the sawmill down to the furniture factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. But this was all within 1 fenced area?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was inside one fence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But part of it was known as the sawmill and part of it was known as the furniture factory?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes, and we built a new fence between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And could you recall whether anything else happened on the evening of the 24th of October, 1993, after you got back to the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yeah. I get back and -- and I get -- we have erect a tent outside so to call it staff tent with communications and I was inside there and talked to my soldiers who was there, some of my officers, and summary what happening the day and checked out what's going on, give order for -- I mean, you couldn't have same soldier outside the whole night so same APCs inside my camp and they have order to some time tonight get out and send back cadavers. So it was about -- I think it was about 10.00 or something like this at the evening. I went into the factory and take my sleeping bag and get ready to sleep, and I have -- I remember I was just to -- going down I have my shoes off. One soldier come inside and said, "Major, major, must came out. They have said we are going to shooting against the Red Cross APC down in Vares if they don't move." And I said, "Don't move them. They should stay there. I don't think they are going to shoot. So let them -- don't move. Stay on the place." And he leaved and in that's moment I talked to myself, so to say, and understand that it's not time for me to go to bed. So I start take my shoe and get ready to get out again, and before I was ready for bed the same soldier come running inside again and said, "You must came. They start shooting in Vares," and in this moment I also could hear it was shooting. And when I come out I could see it was shooting against my positions. I could see flash from weapons. I could also see bullets over the building. And it was -- the situation was not so good in the tent. We was in very high position on the hill and we have nothing to protect us. So my soldier was lying down and talking in radio and it was a lot of talking in radio there. And what's happening was that they threw hand grenades to the Red Cross APC. In the same moment it was two Red Cross APCs. One was going down there to change 10.00. So at this moment it was two Red Cross APCs. And those two APCs was hit with a lot of bullets and two hand grenades. So the wheels -- some of the wheels was destroyed on this vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just ask you this clarification, sir, these, what you've called Red Cross APCs, who owned these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It's a part of my company for wounded soldiers, let's say. They have no arms outside the APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were these vehicles of the International Committee of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: No. It was a number of the UN forces UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what colour were the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: White -- red cross, back side and white near the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you remember after having been awoken and going outside and seeing this shooting?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: The first thing that I do is that in this same time they also have change APC down in the tunnel so it was the APC who was coming back. It was the -- the platoon leader for Alpha platoon. So I gave him radio order to went back and assist these two APCs down in -- in Vares. And also one wheeled APC following after. So it was two APC. One tracked and one with wheel. And they moved down and meet these two Red Cross APC, and we sent them back to the camp and moved down with -- with this in the first vehicle was the tracked APC. And when we came down just before the square it was a lot of shooting against this APC. So they stop, shoot some warning shoot. We were automatic cannon in there. I gave order that if they are shooting against you, I have inform the commander of Bobovac Brigade, so to say, the new commander early at the evening that if you are shooting against us we are going to shooting back, no warning shoot. And what was I gave order? No warning, shoot. If shooting at both you, shoot back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, by the late night of the 24th of October, 1993, had any members of the 8th Mechanised Company been successful in entering Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: No. Nobody had come inside. As I say, before we was outside in this position, I have tell about before, 10.00, and when they start shooting what I have described, we back some 1, maybe 200 metres, stop there, and after that we were staying there the whole night with this tracked APC and one wheeled APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall, Lieutenant Colonel Birger, approximately what time you went to bed on the night of the 24th of October into the 25th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I was not going to bed because we have red alert the whole night of my camp. I have -- I have not so much soldier inside my camp, so all was out digging, and we also have some type of mines, not to -- so to say to kill, only for warning. And we was ready the whole night to -- to fight, because we was afraid. Like I said, we was afraid, because if they -- if they shoot at the Red Cross APCs, if they shoot at my APCs down in Vares, we also could do the second thing. He had warning me to -- with snipers shooting down in the camp because it was a valley and we was -- it was very close to -- to the hill, so to say. So my soldier was out the whole night. Nobody was sleeping. I -- I get to sleep early in the morning inside one Red Cross APC. So I have some hours to sleep, but I wake up about 6.00 or 5.30 like this when we have one more platoon from the 10 Corps also there, another company up in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant Colonel Birger, do you know which force or forces was firing upon the 8th company?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yeah. It was inside Vares, and it was HVO soldiers. We recognised one jeep we had seen before, and it was one jeep staying there, and we also used smoke grenades with phosphor when we draw back and some of this phosphor was also hitting this jeep. So next day we could also see that -- the phosphor, and it was part of the Bobovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about the force or forces that was firing upon your camp in the sawmill do you know?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: No we couldn't see it was dark but if my opinion it was the same forces that shutting down in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, let me break these into two subject areas, one being Stupni Do and one being the school in Vares. Let's talk first, sir, about Stupni Do. What steps did you take on the morning of the 25th of October, 1993, to gain access to the village of Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. We still was -- it was very important for us to came inside Stupni Do, both Stupni Do and the school. So we try again to -- to -- to talk to the Bobovac Brigade to get inside the school, but it was never a thought about that this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Into the --

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: We couldn't come inside this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Into the school.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Stupni Do, okay. So when was the first time tower recollection, sir, that members of the 8th company mechanised company of NordBat were able to get into Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: If I may remember right, I think it was the 26th of -- of October. And we do it in the same way what we have to do the morning of 24th. We do it from two -- two roads. My third platoon, with battalion commander Henricsson on, taken, so to say, the north part, and they was also the first unit who came into Stupni Do. In the same moment when they arrived into Stupni Do, a platoon - it was not from my company, it was from -- I think it was Alpha platoon from the 10 Coy [Realtime transcript read in error "corps"] in Tuzla - I ordered them to passed what we tried to do two days before, over the railway, and they do that, and nobody was shooting against them. So they came in from this road, this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, line 2 of page 86 makes reference to the 10 corps. I believe you said Coy, C-o-y, which is an abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: 10 Coy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Coy being an abbreviation for?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was a company in our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And why did part of the 10th company come down to Vares?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Because I don't have all my soldiers inside my company. Part of them was still outside, and I need more soldiers. This big problem who was growing up day for day in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how did you get these reinforcements from the 10th company.

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: They arrived with tracked APCs, tracked APCs one with wheel down -- at night-time from Tuzla area, and some day later it was one more platoon from this company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, just to be very, very clear for the record, did you personally ever go to the village of Stupni Do in late October?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What information did you receive concerning what NordBat soldiers observed there?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I have immediately the information from my battalion commander that there have been a massacre in Stupni Do. All houses are destroy, still burning here. We could see bodies and so on, so we understand something very, very bad happening in Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the specific people in NordBat who went into Stupni Do on the 26th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yeah. As I said, it was the 3rd platoon, the platoon leader was lieutenant Nilson, and together it was also my commander, my platoon leader for 4th platoon. His soldier wasn't there so he was, so to say, an extra officer with this platoon. It was captain Nilson and, of course, my battalion commander, Colonel Henricsson. It was the first officers who came into Stupni Do, and ti -- together it was 30 soldiers also, and they spread them out immediately to look, to observe what's going -- what's happening inside this village. So very quickly I -- we understand that it is -- what's happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Lieutenant Colonel Birger, whether any medical officers from NordBat entered Stupni Do in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. Later we send in our battalion doctor, so to say, medical staff doctor but it was not this same day. It was later. And the day after we have entered it was some people from Kiseljak where it was military police there to investigate what's happening, and it was also the Chief of Staff of BH command, Brigadier Ramsay, was there, and it was also a lot of media there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who were these people from Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was military police, and the -- and the mission for them was to investigate what's going on, and they have written report about what's happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what military force were these military police from?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant Colonel Birger, let's turn to the school, the situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Mundis. You do not plan this, I think, but you constantly address our witness as Lieutenant Colonel. He has told us that he's a Colonel now, if I understood you correctly, and I do not think there is any reason to downgrade you again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not -- I was Major when I was down in Bosnia. I'm now Lieutenant Colonel. My commander in Bosnia was Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Then there is a mistake in the transcript, because when the president asked you for your grade it is stated that you said Colonel. I apologise, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me turn then to the school in Vares beginning again from the 26th of October 1993, where we left off. What steps -- or the 25th, I'm sorry, the 25th of October. What steps did you take to gain access to the school where the detainees were being kept?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I remember when this platoon arrived at the morning of the 25, I give them order to get down in Vares, so to say, open the road again, take control over the city, and they do that. Then maybe 10.00 or something like this they are reporting that they get down in Vares and they -- nobody was shooting against them. It was more or less very quiet. There is no problem to use the road down. And they send one or two APCs down to the check-point in south and back again. And after that we -- I have this platoon outside the school where we have this prisoner what's mean at the square, and I also arrived with one APC, and we try to use force to get into the school, but it was a lot of HVO soldiers there, and -- and I take a decision it was not to say the right time to use force because we wasn't there to start fighting, and -- and it was also little bit bad position for us. So we wait and put one APC outside the school and leave the area. And the 26th, Sunday, we get into Stupni Do. If I remember right, we also was allowed to visit the prison or in the school, and the officer was Major Daniel Ekberg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
