utterances.text: And Lieutenant Colonel Birger did you visit any of the people in the school?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes but it was some days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what report you received from Major Ekberg following his entry in the school on the 26th of October?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: He described the situation as it was. They were sitting in athletic hall around and they was all of them was more or less beaten up, smashed in the head, in the face, and they was very afraid, and he talked to them and tell them that now, the word now what's going on inside this school, and we do everything to stop what's going on here and try to help you to get out from the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, what he reported to you about the conditions in the school and the conditions of the people who were kept in the school?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. We understand that it was maybe policemen who was there, but we also understand that the people who beat them up was not the policemen, it was young boys who came out, get in and smash them and beaten them up and leave again. And we also have observed that the day before, that is to say traffic in and out of different persons, young boys. So the situation was very bad, and we was afraid they also killed people there, but we don't know in this -- this time we don't know if somebody have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you received any reports about the number of people who were being kept in the school?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yeah. We -- we -- I have -- as I said before, it was 233, 233 people there, and we -- maybe we couldn't say it was so many now there, but it was more than hundreds of people. It was a lot of people inside. Exactly I don't remember if we know how many inside the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant Colonel Birger, do you recall the date that you personally went into the school?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yeah. It was some days later, and I don't really remember exactly the day, but I remember this day all forces from HVO have leaved Vares, leaved the city. We have information that 27 of the prisoner was moved, and -- and -- and -- no, I'm sorry. I'm going to -- to -- one or two days before. When I was there in the beginning, I -- the first time I was in the school it -- they have moved the prisoners so -- to another school. We call it that the south school, and it was south of the city, south part of the city, close to the Catholic church. And I remember also that I was in a mass meeting with commander of Bobovac Brigade. That mean operational officer. And he allow -- he get permission us because we was allowed to get inside the school but only to visit very, short time look and talk to the prisoners, and then we get out again. I don't really remember which day but I think it was somewhere last day in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you -- can you just -- sorry to interrupt, sir. Can you tell us what you saw on that first occasion when you went there?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yeah. We could see the same what we have seen before. They have been beaten up. In the face you could see. Blue eyes, and scars and so on. Blood. They turn off the light so we have to use our hand lights. And up, I want to get upstairs. First they said no, but we discussed with them and we walked up. It was me and one military policeman from my battalion. And we could observe in one room it was blood on the floor. There was also blood in the corridor like you have drawn like a pencil, but if you draw a dead animal, for example, if you draw that with blood you could see some on the floor. It was the same in the stair. So we understand that they have killed bodies. Somebody -- or they have been beaten them up and take them through the corridor out. I also observed that it was -- we -- we ask them. We know, we have information about it 7 -- 27 prisoners is very, very bad. "Where they have these prisoners?" They said, "No, no, they are here." But we could -- we understand that it wasn't like this. So downstairs I could see a door of iron, and I said I want to get inside there and take my lamp and look there, but they stopped me and said, "No, no, there is nothing." And I stopped because I think it was right because there was a lot of bad things lying down there, they haven't used this door for a long time. And some days later we have information about that this 7 -- 27 prisoners was down in an old police station down in the south part of Vares. So we -- we observed in the area and tried to find out which house it was, and -- and -- and one day I think it was -- it was this day what the HVO -- the Bobovac Brigade had leaved Vares, and I think it was the 3rd, maybe, of November. It was the beginning of November. They leaved, but they -- this morning they also burned their headquarter, Bobovac Brigade, and the town -- city was empty of people. Nobody was outside. There was no soldier there. We could hear some single shooting. We won't down to this place called Vares-Majdan, maybe what's the name, and we find this prisoner. They was outside the house. So we take them with us and get up to the south school, and just before I came up there my soldier had opened the school and prisoners was walking outside together with family members. There was also some international media there, and I ordered my soldiers to put up UN flag on the building and we protect the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- you've mentioned this, events about the 3rd of November, roughly, 1993. Can you tell us what else was happening in the town of Vares?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes it was -- it was one house outside Vares was burning. The Bobovac Brigade headquarter, the hotel, was burning. It was a little fire also in the hospital in Vares. That was all. It was -- not much was destroyed. It was -- it was only empty. No soldier there, no people was outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What caused these various fires that were burning?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I think -- I know that one of the families outside had tell me before that, if I leave, I putting fire on my house. So I think it was doing like this. Maybe in the hospital it was a normal accident to have -- it was firing there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about the Bobovac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Bobovac Brigade the evening before I was there because I have been at a meeting up with the deputy commander of the 2nd BH corps in -- I think it was north of Bobovac Brigade's area. And I have also message in a letter to the -- to the leadership of Bobovac Brigade that came here tomorrow as friends or be a part of 2nd Corps. No negotiations. And -- but when I came down to the Bobovac Brigade this evening, it was dark. It was hundred of civilians outside, refugees, so to say, and when I came inside this building it was no commanders there. It was only what I called before, the security officer. He was a little drunk. The people -- soldiers inside there was drinking, and they was burning papers. And next morning it was the whole building on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just to complete this story, sir, what was the next event of any great significance in the town of Vares after the 3rd of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: It was the morning, next morning, very early. The next morning we have information it was forces from the BH army coming from south, and it was some -- also this morning it was some international media team who was leaving my camp, and they came back after some hours or something like this and tell me that they have been looting by -- they take the food and so on. It was soldiers from the BH army, and they was shooting and destroying when we came into the city. So I take one platoon and one -- APCs for my -- as my commanding APCs and get down. And just when we came in front of the square where the mayor house is, what I described before where we also have the first school and the police station, I stopped there, take out my -- my three APCs like a shield, get out and get in front of the soldiers. They came in two lines more or less like in good infantry in this kind of fighting, and there was cross shooting up into the windows and so on and I tried to stop them because there was no necessary to shooting. There were no soldiers there, they only destroy the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there, sir. How many people were left in Vares at this point in time when the ABiH forces entered from the south?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: I -- what I can understand it was thousands of Croats who have leaved. And many of them was down in Dastansko but I also think many have leaved the Serbia area down to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, let me just in the couple of minutes left for this evening ask you about recording of what happened with respect to your unit. Did you keep a personal diary or was there a unit diary that was kept?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: Yeah. Every day we was writing down everything in papers. We signed everything. We send out a patrol, it was signed down. If I gave an order, it was written down. Everything what we do, everything what we observed, everything what's happening was written down in a paper. And in -- when we was down there, my operational officer start written a diary of the company, and he had start already when we was in Denmark, and he finish it when we came home to Sweden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what was done with that diary when it was completed in Sweden --

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: He show me that and I also find somebody -- something I think was not really correct, so I correct so that you have written this and this. And it was not exactly written exactly what's happening. It was more a less a summary for every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was this an official document?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: No. It's only for the soldiers and officers in the company as a memory of the time in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what happened to the official logbooks of the unit?

utterances.speaker: HAKAN BIRGER
utterances.text: What I can understand they sent to -- we have them in -- in Sweden. We take them every month for something like this, but I don't really exactly where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I would require approximately 15 minutes tomorrow morning simply to go through about 10 documents with the witness and then that would complete the examination-in-chief, but I don't believe we could even start that efficiently at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Well, it's time to stop. It's almost 7.00 p.m. As you know, we're sitting in the morning this week, so we will resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
